# Bonus: NTP Time Synchronization {.unnumbered}

Over the span of several months, even a highly accurate RTC like our DS3231 will inevitably drift by a few seconds. Since we're already connecting to the internet to upload our weather data, we have an amazing opportunity to perform some self-healing!

In this bonus chapter, we will implement **Network Time Protocol (NTP)** synchronization. Whenever our weather station successfully connects to Wi-Fi and uploads data, it will immediately query a global atomic clock server and transparently recalibrate the DS3231.

## How NTP Works

NTP is the standard protocol that computers use to synchronize their clocks over the internet. The ESP32's core libraries make this incredibly easy via the `configTime()` function.

1. The ESP32 connects to an NTP server pool (e.g., `pool.ntp.org`).
2. The server responds with the exact current Unix timestamp.
3. The ESP32 formats it into a C-style `struct tm` time object.
4. We write this newly acquired, perfectly accurate time back to the DS3231.

> **Timezone Considerations:** It is universally considered best practice in IoT to store and transmit timestamps in **UTC (Universal Coordinated Time)**, which effectively represents the time in Greenwich, London, without Daylight Saving Time. We will set our timezone offset to `0`. If you want to view the data in your local timezone, you should apply the offset on your backend dashboard (like Grafana), not on the edge device!

## The Code

> **Ready-to-use project:** The complete code for this time synchronization firmware is available in the repository here: [`08_ntp_sync`](https://github.com/wg1d/personal-autonomous-weather-station/tree/main/firmware/Phase-03/08_ntp_sync)

To enable NTP, we simply include the `<time.h>` library at the top of the file:

```cpp
#include <time.h>
```

In **Path B** (Standard Wakeup), right after we successfully upload the CSV to our dummy backend server and before we disconnect from Wi-Fi, we run our self-healing logic:

```cpp
// Bonus: NTP Time Synchronization
Serial.println("Synchronizing DS3231 RTC with NTP...");
configTime(0, 0, "pool.ntp.org"); // Offset 0 for UTC

struct tm timeinfo;
if (getLocalTime(&timeinfo, 5000)) { // 5-second timeout
  Serial.println("NTP Time acquired!");
  
  time_t ntpUnix = mktime(&timeinfo);
  uint32_t rtcUnix = rtc.now().unixtime();
  
  // Only update if drift is greater than 2 seconds
  if (abs((long)(ntpUnix - rtcUnix)) > 2) {
    Serial.println("Drift detected! Updating RTC...");
    rtc.adjust(DateTime(timeinfo.tm_year + 1900, timeinfo.tm_mon + 1, timeinfo.tm_mday, 
                        timeinfo.tm_hour, timeinfo.tm_min, timeinfo.tm_sec));
  } else {
    Serial.println("RTC time is accurate. No update needed.");
  }
} else {
  Serial.println("Failed to obtain time from NTP server.");
}
```

### Understanding the Code
- `configTime(gmtOffset, daylightOffset, server)`: Configures the internal ESP32 SNTP client. We pass `0` for both offsets to lock our station to UTC, and we use `pool.ntp.org` as our atomic clock source.
- `getLocalTime(&timeinfo, 5000)`: Attempts to fetch the time into the `timeinfo` structure. If the network is slow, it gives up after 5000 milliseconds (5 seconds) to prevent draining the battery.
- **The Drift Check:** Why do we only update if the drift is greater than 2 seconds? Whenever you call `rtc.adjust()`, the DS3231 completely resets its internal sub-second counter to zero. If you call this function every single time the ESP32 wakes up, you artificially force the clock to lose a fraction of a second over and over again, *causing* more drift than you fix! By only updating when the drift exceeds 2 seconds, we allow the RTC to run naturally and only intervene when absolutely necessary.

## Running the Test

To prove that our self-healing logic actually works, we need to intentionally break the clock!

1. In the `setup()` function of `08_ntp_sync.ino`, temporarily add `rtc.adjust(DateTime(2000, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0));` right after `rtc.begin()`.
2. Compile and upload the code.
3. Remove the line you just added, and upload it again. Your ESP32 is now trapped in the year 2000!
4. Watch the Serial Monitor as it wakes up, reads the sensors, connects to Wi-Fi, uploads the data, and triggers the NTP sync.

### Expected Output

```text
--- Waking up from Deep Sleep ---
Standard Wakeup (RTC Timer). Taking reading...
Data: 2000-01-01T00:00:30;29.41;32.10;990.87
Data saved to SD card.
Connecting to WiFi...
Connected to WiFi network
Uploading CSV file to server: http://192.168.1.15:5000/upload
HTTP Response code: 200
Synchronizing DS3231 RTC with NTP...
NTP Time acquired!
Drift detected! Updating RTC...
Next reading scheduled for: 17:15:00
Entering Deep Sleep...
```

Notice that the initial timestamp was `2000-01-01`, but right before going to sleep, it fetched the atomic time and instantly snapped the schedule forward to the real time (`17:15:00`)!

Congratulations! Your autonomous weather station is now completely maintenance-free, self-healing, and perpetually locked to the atomic clock grid!

## Next Steps

With NTP synchronization complete, our feature set for the ESP32 is fully realized! However, as we've added sensors, SD cards, sleep logic, and Wi-Fi, our codebase has grown into a massive, monolithic file. 

In **Phase 4: Firmware Architecture**, we will pause adding new features and instead refactor our code into a clean, modular architecture (separating headers and source files) to make it maintainable for the future!
